issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
Mika is a 55-year-old Pacific Islander man who has been working as a nanny for several years, caring for two young children in a busy American household after his own divorce. He came to treatment carrying the aftermath of a trauma centered on someone he loved, and when he tries to speak about it directly, his account breaks apart. He begins, stops, doubles back, and loses the thread, as if the most important moments cannot be held in order long enough to be told. Even in early sessions, it is clear that this is not reluctance so much as the way the memory comes to him: in broken pieces, with sound and grief arriving faster than words.

The event involved a loved one suffering catastrophic bodily injury in front of him. What remains most vivid to Mika is not a coherent sequence but a set of unbearable impressions: the sight of the injured body, the particular body parts that were damaged, and the sounds he heard in those moments. When the memory comes back, he does not simply “think about” what happened. He hears it again in his head, as though the frightening event has its own soundtrack that returns without warning. Those sounds are inseparable from a crushing sense of loss. He says that remembering does not feel like remembering in the ordinary sense; it feels like being struck by grief all over again.

In the weeks after the trauma, Mika found that certain reminders could undo him almost instantly. Images involving specific body parts associated with what he witnessed were especially potent. A glimpse of an injury on television, a medical scene, even ordinary visual details that resembled what he had seen could make his chest tighten and his mind flood with the scene. Reminders of victims in general had a similar effect. News stories, memorial photographs, or even the sight of someone looking frail or hurt could pull him back toward the same unbearable mental fragments. Talk about people losing loved ones became difficult to tolerate. If another parent at the playground mentioned a death in the family, or if the children’s mother discussed a bereaved friend within earshot, Mika would go quiet and feel himself slipping away from the present. He often excused himself to the kitchen or bathroom, not because he did not care, but because the theme of loss landed with such force that it became hard to remain composed.

His work as a nanny has made these moments hard to avoid completely. Children notice bodies, ask blunt questions, and sometimes come home describing playground injuries or scenes from shows they have watched. Mika has become especially tense around these conversations. If one of the children points to a scraped knee or talks about someone being hurt, he may respond too quickly, steering the conversation elsewhere. At times he has avoided certain books or programs if they contain illness, injury, or death. The parents have noticed that he becomes unusually still when such topics arise. Over time, this has narrowed his ease with the family. He remains dependable and caring, but more guarded, more likely to keep his inner life sealed off.

Alongside these moments, Mika has developed harsh beliefs about himself. He has come to believe he is a weak person, and he says this with shame rather than anger. In his mind, a stronger man would have done more, acted faster, protected the person he loved. What haunts him most is the conviction that he failed to protect others. He returns again and again to what he should have done, even though when he tries to describe the event fully, language deserts him. This self-judgment sits beside another painful change in how he experiences himself: he often feels less like a person than like an object, as if some essential human quality has been stripped away. In those moments he moves through the day performing tasks, packing lunches, folding children’s clothes, walking them home, but with a deadened sense that he is only functioning mechanically.

Months turned into longer habits of constriction. Mika limited what he watched, what conversations he entered, and how much he disclosed. He kept his grief largely private. His divorce had already left him with a thinner sense of support, and after the trauma he withdrew further, not wanting to break down in front of others or be asked to explain what he could not explain clearly himself. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single new crisis but the accumulation of these moments at work and in daily life: too many times stepping away when loss was mentioned, too many occasions when an image of an injured body part caught him off guard, too many nights left shaken by sounds replaying in his head. He came in frightened that this was what he had become now, a weak man who had failed someone he loved and no longer felt fully human. At the same time, he was hoping for something modest but urgent: to be able to remember without falling apart, and to stay present with the people who still need him.
